llm_response.content:
Empirical Research Plan  
“School-district competition, student achievement, and taxpayer cost”

------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy  
Strategy: Two–stage least squares (panel IV) with district and year fixed effects.  

Why IV?  
• Competition is endogenous: high-quality districts may induce either (i) defensive consolidation of neighboring districts or (ii) parental sorting that changes the number of effective rivals.  
• The institutional context delivers plausibly exogenous, long-run variation in potential competition that is rooted in geography and history.  
• A cross-district, multi-year panel with fixed effects allows us to difference out time-invariant unobservables and common shocks, while IV purges remaining endogeneity in the competition measure.

Instrument: “Pre-determined fragmentation” – the number of independent school districts that existed in 1940 within today’s metropolitan boundaries, interacted with post-1990 population growth of the metro.  
• 1940 fragmentation is fixed long before modern accountability or choice policies.  
• Interaction with contemporary population growth creates time-varying, local, exogenous pressure for competition: as population expands inside historically fragmented metros, parents can choose among many nearby districts, whereas equally-growing metros with historically consolidated districts remain low-choice.  
• This follows the “Bartik/shift–share” logic: historical shares × current shocks.

Robustness/validation:  
• A difference-in-differences event study around state-level open-enrollment laws is a complementary design check but is not the primary identification device.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control  

Treatment variable (continuous):  
Comp_{it} = (1 – HHI_{it}) where HHI_{it} is the Herfindahl index of enrollment shares of all traditional public districts operating inside a 30-minute drive-time of district i in year t. Higher Comp means more competition.

Instrument (Z_{mt}) at metropolitan (m) × year (t) level:  
Z_{mt} = HistoricDistricts_{m,1940} × PopGrowth_{mt}  
Then assign Z_{mt} to each district i ∈ m.

Counterfactual: Districts that face lower instrument-predicted competition (bottom quartile of Z) serve as the comparison group for districts in higher quartiles, but estimation is continuous.

Timing: The interaction term varies annually because PopGrowth_{mt} is cumulative population since 1990, so treatment “intensity” evolves over time; there is no single cutoff date.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

A1. Relevance: Historic fragmentation interacted with population growth strongly predicts today’s competition (first-stage F-stat ≫ 10). Plausible: more historical districts + more people implies more extant rivals.  

A2. Exclusion: Historic fragmentation affects current outcomes only through its effect on current competition, not through other channels (e.g., institutional culture, persistent wealth). Plausible because (i) we include district fixed effects that soak up time-invariant historic traits, and (ii) metropolitan-year controls (income, racial composition, unemployment) capture evolving local shocks.  

A3. Monotonicity: In metros where population grows, historic fragmentation cannot systematically reduce competition (no “defiers”). Highly plausible.  

A4. SUTVA: One district’s potential outcomes depend only on its own level of competition, not the instrument of another metro. Reasonable across metros; within metro interactions are internalized by Comp_{it}.  

A5. Parallel trends in controls: For DID robustness, treated and control metros would have followed parallel trends absent policy. Plausible once district and year fixed effects plus metro-specific linear trends are added.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Threats to Identification & Mitigations  

T1. Omitted metro-level shocks correlated with historical fragmentation (e.g., legacy industrial base) influence both education spending and outcomes.  
Mitigation: Add metro-year controls (income per capita, unemployment, age structure), include metro-specific linear or quadratic trends, and perform a “placebo” using pre-1990 outcomes where modern competition is minimal to verify zero reduced-form effects.

T2. Residential sorting: Families with higher preferences for education may move into high-competition metros, biasing results upward.  
Mitigation: (i) Fixed district dummies remove time-invariant selection; (ii) control for time-varying demographic composition (% FRPL, % minority); (iii) estimate bounds using Lee (2009) “trimming” on observables; (iv) an additional IV that uses geographic barriers (river miles, coastline) as an alternative instrument assesses robustness.

T3. Measurement error in Comp_{it} arising from mis-defined drive-time markets or missing charter enrollment.  
Mitigation: (i) Use multiple market definitions (10, 20, 30 miles) as sensitivity checks; (ii) supplement with NCES Common Core and charter files to capture rivals; (iii) errors-in-variables bias is attenuated in 2SLS.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline  

```r
# === 0. Packages ===
library(tidyverse)
library(fixest)        # fast two–way FE & IV
library(estimatr)      # robust IV SEs
library(modelsummary)

# === 1. Load data ===
dist   <- read_csv("district_panel.csv")      # district-year observations
metro  <- read_csv("metro_covariates.csv")    # metro-year covariates
hist40 <- read_csv("historic_districts_1940.csv")  # metro-level historic counts

# === 2. Merge & construct variables ===
data <- dist %>% 
  left_join(metro,  by = c("metro", "year")) %>%
  left_join(hist40, by = "metro") %>%
  group_by(metro) %>% 
  mutate(pop_growth = population - population[year == 1990]) %>%
  ungroup() %>% 
  mutate(competition   = 1 - hhi,                       # treatment
         instrument    = hist_districts_1940 * pop_growth,
         ln_spending   = log(total_spending_per_pupil),
         test_z        = (avg_math + avg_read)/2)       # outcome

# === 3. Main 2SLS specification ===
iv_main <- feols(test_z ~ 1 | district + year ~ competition | instrument, 
                 data = data, cluster = ~metro)
etable(iv_main, title = "Main 2SLS: Competition on Student Achievement")

# === 4. Cost outcome ===
iv_cost <- feols(ln_spending ~ 1 | district + year ~ competition | instrument,
                 data = data, cluster = ~metro)

# === 5. Robustness: alternative market radius ===
data_alt <- read_csv("district_panel_radius20.csv")  # HHI built on 20-mile radius
data_alt <- data_alt %>% 
  left_join(metro,  by = c("metro", "year")) %>%
  left_join(hist40, by = "metro") %>%
  mutate(pop_growth = population - population[year == 1990],
         competition20 = 1 - hhi20,
         instrument    = hist_districts_1940 * pop_growth)

iv_alt <- feols(test_z ~ 1 | district + year ~ competition20 | instrument,
                data = data_alt, cluster = ~metro)

# === 6. Summarise results ===
modelsummary(list(Main = iv_main, Alt_Radius = iv_alt, Cost = iv_cost),
             stars = TRUE, output = "markdown")
```

------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results  

Theory (Tiebout & Hirschman): more choice/exit options induce districts to compete on quality and cost-efficiency.  
Hypothesis:  
• Student achievement: β_1 > 0. Rough prior: A 0.10 increase in (1–HHI) raises mean test z-score by ≈ 0.05 SD.  
• Cost: β_2 < 0. A 0.10 increase in (1–HHI) lowers log spending per pupil by ≈ 2–4 percent.  
Combined, we expect better outcomes at equal or lower taxpayer cost → efficiency gains.

------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (IV design)  

C1: Instrument relevance (first-stage F>10) ………………… 1  
C2: Exclusion restriction credible …………………………….. 0.5  
C3: No differential trends after controls …………………….. 0.5  
C4: Monotonicity (no defiers) …………………………………… 1  
C5: SUTVA (no spillovers across metros) …………………… 0.5  

Total score = 3.5 / 5 – design is reasonably strong but rests on a contestable exclusion restriction and the possibility of residual spillovers/trends, which will be probed through robustness and placebo tests.
